claims.claim: Nested shrinkage gives better par scores than raw ground averages, especially for small samples.
claims.test: Fit par on a random 70% of clean matches; predict the first-innings total of the other 30% from (a) the raw ground-season average, (b) the shrunk par, (c) the competition average, (d) one global average. Lower RMSE is better.
claims.numbers: RMSE in runs: shrunk 33.06, raw ground-season 35.23, competition mean 34.43, global 34.56. Raw minus shrunk, 95% bootstrap interval 1.34 to 3.05 runs. Ground-seasons with under 5 innings: raw 35.68, shrunk 32.03 (395 test innings). Without our between-variance correction: 33.22.
claims.rule: confirmed if the bootstrap interval for raw minus shrunk RMSE is above 0 and shrunk par also beats one global average; partly if it only beats the raw averages
claims.our_miss: The gain over a plain competition average is small (1.37 runs): most of a total's spread is match-to-match noise that no par can remove.

claims.claim: The same shrinkage transfers to 8-a-side, 5-ball-over club cricket.
claims.test: Same held-out test on Last Man Stands matches (division, season, ground).
claims.numbers: RMSE: shrunk 32.36, raw 32.7, division mean 32.43, global 31.87; raw minus shrunk 95% interval 0.1 to 0.57.
claims.rule: confirmed if the bootstrap interval is above 0 and shrunk par also beats one global average; partly if it only beats the raw averages
claims.our_miss: In club cricket, ground and division explain almost nothing on held-out games: one league-wide average predicts as well as any par. Shrinkage still protects against the raw averages' small samples.

claims.claim: A game-state baseline (balls left, wickets, par/target, innings) tracks actual runs per ball over by over, in both high- and low-par conditions.
claims.test: Fit the baseline on 70% of matches; on the other 30%, compare actual and expected first-innings runs per ball by over, for par above 185.0 and below 160.0.
claims.numbers: High par: actual 1.46 v expected 1.514 runs per ball, largest gap in any over 0.21. Low par: actual 1.249 v expected 1.236, largest gap 0.133. All: mean gap per over 0.024.
claims.rule: confirmed if every over is within 0.12 runs per ball and the baseline is higher in high-par conditions
claims.our_miss: We use binned, shrunk averages rather than the primer's gradient-boosted model; a single over of a few hundred balls can still be off by a tenth of a run.

claims.claim: A DL-style curve with cubic F(w) and beta(w) fits T20 runs-to-come; a full innings is worth about 170 and beta(0) is about 140 balls.
claims.test: Weighted least squares on every first-innings (balls left, wickets) cell; compare the headline constants and the shape with the published DL table rescaled to T20.
claims.numbers: R(120,0) = 169.86; beta(0) = 132.8 balls; weighted RMSE of cell means 1.034 runs over 847 cells. At 10 overs left our curve gives 61.1% (0 down) and 24.1% (7 down) against DL's 56.7% and 31.6%.
claims.rule: confirmed if R(120,0) is within 5 runs of 170 and beta(0) within 20% of 140
claims.our_miss: A small soft-penalty violation remains: with one or two balls left, runs to come rise by up to about 0.03 runs between 0 and 3 down.

claims.claim: High-scoring conditions 'straighten' the curve: lambda stretches it with an exponent n0 = 1.04, front-loading the scoring.
claims.test: Fit n0 on first innings in the top quarter of par (par >= 176.7), re-solving lambda from par for each candidate; compare runs-to-come errors.
claims.rule: not confirmed if the best-fitting n0 is below 0.5 and fits better than 1.04
claims.our_miss: In our data a higher par mostly scales the whole curve up; the difference in fit is small, so this is weak evidence either way.

claims.claim: Worked example: at 60-2 after 6 overs with par 180, a four is worth about +3.08 runs and a wicket about -11.8.
claims.test: Recompute the example with our independently fitted curve.
claims.n: curve fitted on all clean pro matches
claims.rule: confirmed if the four is within 0.3 runs and the wicket within 1 run of the primer

claims.claim: The sum of Impact over an innings equals runs scored above the expected total R(120,0,lambda).
claims.test: Sum ball Impact for every first innings and subtract (total - R(120,0,lambda)).
claims.numbers: Mean difference -0.001 runs; largest 2.0 (penalty runs not on any ball).
claims.rule: holds by construction (the sum telescopes); confirmed if mean is within 0.05

claims.claim: The match difference in Impact maps to win probability through a logistic curve with slope about 0.25 per run.
claims.test: Fit a logistic regression of the result on the Impact gap between the sides. Note: because we do not cap the chase, a winning chase banks its unused resources, so the sign of the gap matches the result by construction.
claims.numbers: With our definitions the gap has the same sign as the result in 100.0% of matches, so the slope is not finite (fit returned 27.806). Using only the first innings' Impact: slope 0.0445 per run.
claims.rule: not confirmed if we cannot reproduce a finite slope near 0.25
claims.our_miss: Probably a definitional difference: with the uncapped chase, a side that wins a chase banks its unused resources, which makes the gap almost decide the result. The primer's exact match-level definition is not given.

claims.claim: Impact rate is close to a linear mix of strike rate and average: IR = -106.7 + 0.713 SR + 0.293 Avg, R^2 0.75 (batter-seasons with 200+ balls).
claims.test: Ordinary least squares on our batter-seasons with 200+ balls, all five competitions.
claims.rule: confirmed if R^2 is within 0.1 of 0.75 and the SR weight within 0.15 of 0.713

claims.claim: The Pythagorean form r^n / (1 + r^n) fits best with n = 6 in both innings.
claims.test: Maximum likelihood for n on 70% of matches.
claims.rule: confirmed if both fitted exponents are within 1 of 6

claims.claim: The model is well calibrated (primer: Brier 0.182, ECE 0.0177, close to Cricinfo's forecaster) and discriminates (AUC 0.703 first innings, 0.809 second).
claims.test: Score the 30% held-out matches; 15 equal-count bins; Brier, log-loss, AUC, expected calibration error (ECE).
claims.numbers: n = 6, both innings: Brier 0.1743, ECE 0.0196, AUC 0.8165. By innings with n = 6: ECE 0.0439 and 0.0388; AUC 0.7183 and 0.9016. Batting-first sides won 46.2% of test matches. After our Platt shift: ECE 0.0225 and 0.0245, both innings 0.0127.
claims.rule: confirmed if ECE <= 0.03 overall and in each innings with n = 6; partly if only overall
claims.our_miss: Our first version used n = 6 alone and missed our own per-innings target (ECE 0.03); the fitted shift fixes it.

claims.claim: The same win-probability method works for Last Man Stands.
claims.test: Same held-out calibration on LMS matches.
claims.numbers: Platt-shifted: Brier 0.1718, ECE 0.0118, AUC 0.8209; n = 6 form: ECE 0.0138.
claims.rule: confirmed if held-out ECE <= 0.03; partly if <= 0.06
claims.our_miss: Small test set: bins hold a few hundred balls each.

claims.claim: Season WPA reads as 'matches won'; the top IPL 2026 batter and bowler added about 1.71 and 1.70.
claims.test: Sum WPA by player for IPL 2026 (our latest IPL season in Cricsheet).
claims.numbers: Top batter 1.91, top bowler 1.42. WPA per match sums exactly to the result: largest error 0.0.
claims.rule: confirmed if both leaders are within 0.5 wins of the primer
claims.our_miss: Different win-probability calibration (our Platt shift) moves individual totals slightly.

claims.claim: Leverage is highest in the first-innings powerplay and falls; in the chase it is spread out with the highest values in the last overs.
claims.test: Mean leverage index by over and innings, all pro matches.
claims.numbers: 1st innings: over 1 1.449, over 20 0.488. 2nd innings: over 1 1.0, peak 1.453 in the last four overs; 90th percentile at over 20 6.594.
claims.rule: confirmed if the first-innings peak is in the powerplay and the chase peak is in the last 4 overs

claims.claim: WPA and |WPA| do not scale with leverage, so WPA should not be divided by leverage.
claims.test: Mean |WPA| per ball in deciles of leverage index.
claims.numbers: |WPA| rises from 0.0011 in the lowest decile to 0.0367 in the highest; correlation of LI with |WPA| 0.433.
claims.rule: not confirmed if the correlation between LI and |WPA| is above 0.2
claims.our_miss: May depend on how the primer binned or defined |WPA|; we only see the summary sentence.

claims.test: The primer has no definition yet ('in preparation').
claims.numbers: T20 Lab shows its own clutch measure, clearly labelled, without claiming it is the primer's.

claims.claim: Game state predicts runs per ball better than line, length or seam (from the video).
claims.test: Needs ball-tracking data, which Cricsheet does not have.
